1553: ===== documents/matters/1006-00005/Settlement/settlement-agreement-and-mutual-release.docx =====
1554: **[SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT AND MUTUAL RELEASE]{.underline}**
1555: 
1556: **Effective Date: December 3, 2021**
1557: 
1558: This Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release (this \"Agreement\") is entered into as of December 3, 2021 (the \"Effective Date\"), by and between:
1559: 
1560: **CRESTLINE PACKAGING SOLUTIONS LLC**, an Ohio limited liability company, with its principal place of business at 4500 Needmore Road, Dayton, OH 45424 (\"CPS\");
1561: 
1562: and
1563: 
1564: **RIDGEWAY FREIGHT SERVICES INC.**, a Texas corporation, with its principal place of business at 7200 East Lancaster Avenue, Fort Worth, TX 76112 (\"Ridgeway\").
1565: 
1566: CPS and Ridgeway are each referred to herein individually as a \"Party\" and collectively as the \"Parties.\"
1567: 
1568: **[RECITALS]{.underline}**
1569: 
1570: **WHEREAS**, on April 15, 2019, CPS and Ridgeway entered into that certain Master Transportation Services Agreement (the \"MTSA\"), pursuant to which Ridgeway agreed to provide full truckload and less-than-truckload freight transportation services to CPS, including intrastate and interstate linehaul, cross-docking, and last-mile delivery services, in accordance with the rates, routes, and service levels specified therein;
1571: 
1572: **WHEREAS**, CPS terminated the MTSA effective April 22, 2021, pursuant to Section 9.2 thereof, following CPS\'s issuance of a thirty (30)-day written termination notice to Ridgeway on March 22, 2021;
1573: 
1574: **WHEREAS**, on or about June 7, 2021, CPS filed a lawsuit styled *Crestline Packaging Solutions LLC v. Ridgeway Freight Services Inc.*, Cause No. 342-2021-04871-TX, in the 342nd Judicial District Court of Tarrant County, Texas (the \"Lawsuit\"), asserting claims for breach of contract, money had and received, common-law fraud, and unjust enrichment, and seeking recovery of One Million Eight Hundred Forty-Seven Thousand Six Hundred Thirty-Two Dollars and Nineteen Cents (\$1,847,632.19) in alleged overcharges, together with contractual interest, attorneys\' fees, costs of court, and exemplary damages;
1575: 
1576: **WHEREAS**, Ridgeway filed a counterclaim in the Lawsuit asserting breach of contract based on CPS\'s alleged wrongful termination of the MTSA, seeking recovery of Three Hundred Forty Thousand Dollars (\$340,000.00) in alleged lost profits and related consequential damages;
1577: 
1578: **WHEREAS**, the Parties participated in a mediation before the Honorable Constance Farr, Judge (Ret.), at the Lone Star Dispute Resolution Center, 300 Throckmorton Street, Suite 1200, Fort Worth, TX 76102, on November 18, 2021, and, as a result of that mediation, reached an agreement in principle to resolve all claims and counterclaims asserted in the Lawsuit;
1579: 
1580: **WHEREAS**, the Parties desire to fully, finally, and forever resolve all disputes, controversies, claims, and counterclaims between them arising out of or relating to the MTSA, the Lawsuit, and any and all transactions and occurrences described therein, and to avoid the expense, burden, uncertainty, and distraction of further litigation; and
1581: 
1582: **NOW, THEREFORE**, in consideration of the mutual promises, covenants, and agreements set forth herein, and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged by each Party, the Parties agree as follows:
1583: 
1584: **[ARTICLE I --- SETTLEMENT PAYMENT]{.underline}**
1585: 
1586: **Section 1.1 --- Settlement Amount**
1587: 
1588: Ridgeway shall pay to CPS the total sum of One Million Five Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars (\$1,575,000.00) (the \"Settlement Amount\"), subject to and in accordance with the payment schedule set forth below:
1589: 
1590: > **(a) First Installment.** One Million Dollars (\$1,000,000.00) shall be due and payable within thirty (30) calendar days of the Effective Date (i.e., no later than January 2, 2022). Such payment shall be made by wire transfer of immediately available funds to a bank account designated in writing by CPS in accordance with Section 1.3 below.
1591: >
1592: > **(b) Second Installment.** Five Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars (\$575,000.00) shall be due and payable within ninety (90) calendar days of the Effective Date (i.e., no later than March 3, 2022). Such payment shall be made by wire transfer of immediately available funds to a bank account designated in writing by CPS in accordance with Section 1.3 below.
1593: 
1594: The Settlement Amount shall be allocated and reported for tax purposes in accordance with applicable law, and each Party shall be solely responsible for its own tax obligations arising from or relating to the receipt or payment of the Settlement Amount. Neither Party makes any representation or warranty to the other regarding the tax treatment or tax consequences of the Settlement Amount or any portion thereof.
1595: 
1596: **Section 1.2 --- Late Payment**
1597: 
1598: In the event that Ridgeway fails to make any installment payment when due as set forth in Section 1.1, interest shall accrue on the unpaid amount at the rate of one and one-half percent (1.5%) per month (eighteen percent (18%) per annum) from the applicable due date until such payment, together with all accrued interest thereon, is paid in full. Such interest shall compound monthly on the last calendar day of each month.
1599: 
1600: Upon any payment default by Ridgeway that remains uncured for ten (10) business days following written notice of such default from CPS to Ridgeway in accordance with Section 7.8, CPS shall be entitled, at its sole option and in addition to any other remedies available at law or in equity, to enter a consent judgment against Ridgeway in the amount of the entire unpaid balance of the Settlement Amount, plus all accrued and unpaid interest thereon, plus CPS\'s reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs incurred in connection with the enforcement of this Agreement (collectively, the \"Judgment Amount\"). Ridgeway hereby irrevocably consents to the entry of such judgment in the 342nd Judicial District Court of Tarrant County, Texas, and irrevocably waives any objection to personal jurisdiction, subject-matter jurisdiction, or venue in connection therewith. The Parties acknowledge that this consent judgment provision is a material inducement to CPS\'s agreement to accept installment payments rather than a single lump-sum payment, and that the enforcement rights set forth in this Section 1.2 are reasonable and necessary to protect CPS\'s legitimate interests under this Agreement.
1601: 
1602: **Section 1.3 --- Wire Instructions**
1603: 
1604: CPS shall provide Ridgeway with complete wire transfer instructions, including the name and address of the receiving financial institution, the ABA routing number, account name, and account number, within five (5) business days of the Effective Date. Ridgeway shall be entitled to rely on such instructions until CPS provides updated instructions in writing. Any change to wire transfer instructions must be confirmed by telephone by CPS\'s General Counsel or his designee prior to Ridgeway acting upon such changed instructions.
1605: 
1606: **[ARTICLE II --- MUTUAL RELEASES]{.underline}**
1607: 
1608: **Section 2.1 --- Release by CPS**
1609: 
1610: Effective upon CPS\'s receipt of the full Settlement Amount (including both the First Installment and the Second Installment as set forth in Section 1.1), CPS, on behalf of itself and its members, managers, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"CPS Releasing Parties\"), hereby fully, finally, unconditionally, and irrevocably releases, acquits, and forever discharges Ridgeway and its shareholders, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, insurers, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"Ridgeway Released Parties\") from any and all claims, demands, actions, causes of action, suits, debts, dues, sums of money, accounts, reckonings, bonds, bills, specialties, covenants, contracts, controversies, agreements, promises, variances, trespasses, judgments, executions, obligations, damages, losses, costs, expenses, and liabilities of every kind and nature whatsoever, whether at law or in equity, whether arising under statute, contract, tort, or otherwise, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, fixed or contingent, matured or unmatured, liquidated or unliquidated, that the CPS Releasing Parties ever had, now have, or hereafter may have against the Ridgeway Released Parties, from the beginning of the world through the Effective Date, arising out of, relating to, or in any way connected with: (i) the MTSA, including all amendments, schedules, and addenda thereto; (ii) the Lawsuit, including all claims, counterclaims, cross-claims, and defenses asserted or that could have been asserted therein; or (iii) the transactions, services, invoices, payments, disputes, negotiations, communications, and events described in or relating to the MTSA or the Lawsuit.
1611: 
1612: **Section 2.2 --- Release by Ridgeway**
1613: 
1614: Effective as of the Effective Date, Ridgeway, on behalf of itself and its shareholders, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, insurers, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"Ridgeway Releasing Parties\"), hereby fully, finally, unconditionally, and irrevocably releases, acquits, and forever discharges CPS and its members, managers, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"CPS Released Parties\") from any and all claims, demands, actions, causes of action, suits, debts, dues, sums of money, accounts, reckonings, bonds, bills, specialties, covenants, contracts, controversies, agreements, promises, variances, trespasses, judgments, executions, obligations, damages, losses, costs, expenses, and liabilities of every kind and nature whatsoever, whether at law or in equity, whether arising under statute, contract, tort, or otherwise, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, fixed or contingent, matured or unmatured, liquidated or unliquidated, that the Ridgeway Releasing Parties ever had, now have, or hereafter may have against the CPS Released Parties, from the beginning of the world through the Effective Date, arising out of, relating to, or in any way connected with: (i) the MTSA, including all amendments, schedules, and addenda thereto; (ii) the Lawsuit, including all claims, counterclaims, cross-claims, and defenses asserted or that could have been asserted therein; or (iii) the transactions, services, invoices, payments, disputes, negotiations, communications, and events described in or relating to the MTSA or the Lawsuit. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the release set forth in this Section 2.2 specifically encompasses and includes Ridgeway\'s counterclaim for alleged lost profits of Three Hundred Forty Thousand Dollars (\$340,000.00) and any and all other claims for damages, whether direct, indirect, consequential, incidental, ... (line truncated to 2000 chars)
1615: 
1616: The Parties acknowledge and agree that Ridgeway\'s release under this Section 2.2 is effective immediately upon the Effective Date and is not conditioned upon CPS\'s receipt of the Settlement Amount or any installment thereof.
1617: 
1618: **Section 2.3 --- Reservation**
1619: 
1620: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, the releases set forth therein shall not release, waive, or otherwise affect:
1621: 
1622: > \(a\) the Parties\' respective rights, obligations, covenants, and duties under this Agreement, all of which shall survive the execution and delivery of this Agreement in accordance with their terms; or
1623: >
1624: > \(b\) any claims, demands, actions, or causes of action arising from or related to a breach of this Agreement by either Party.
1625: 
1626: **[ARTICLE III --- DISMISSAL]{.underline}**
1627: 
1628: **Section 3.1 --- Dismissal**
1629: 
1630: Within ten (10) business days of the Effective Date, the Parties shall cause their respective counsel to jointly prepare, execute, and file an Agreed Order of Dismissal with Prejudice (the \"Dismissal Order\") in Cause No. 342-2021-04871-TX, pending in the 342nd Judicial District Court of Tarrant County, Texas. The Dismissal Order shall dismiss all of CPS\'s claims and all of Ridgeway\'s counterclaims with prejudice and without costs to either Party, with each Party bearing its own costs and attorneys\' fees except as otherwise expressly provided in this Agreement. Counsel for CPS, Calderwood & Harkness LLP, shall prepare the initial draft of the Dismissal Order and shall submit such draft to counsel for Ridgeway, Bartlett, Hogue & Sinclair LLP, for review and approval as to form prior to filing. Counsel for Ridgeway shall provide any comments or indicate approval as to form within five (5) business days of receipt of the draft Dismissal Order. The Parties shall cooperate fully and in good faith to secure entry of the Dismissal Order by the Court as expeditiously as practicable.
1631: 
1632: **[ARTICLE IV --- CONFIDENTIALITY]{.underline}**
1633: 
1634: **Section 4.1 --- Confidentiality**
1635: 
1636: The Parties agree that the existence and terms of this Agreement, including without limitation the Settlement Amount and the payment schedule, are and shall remain strictly confidential. Except as expressly provided in this Section 4.1, neither Party shall disclose, publicize, or disseminate, directly or indirectly, the terms, conditions, or substance of this Agreement to any third party. Notwithstanding the foregoing, either Party may disclose the terms of this Agreement:
1637: 
1638: > \(a\) to such Party\'s legal, financial, and tax advisors, including outside counsel, accountants, and tax preparers, who shall be informed of and bound by the confidentiality obligations set forth in this Section 4.1 as a condition of such disclosure;
1639: >
1640: > \(b\) to such Party\'s auditors, lenders, insurers, or investors, on a need-to-know basis and subject to appropriate confidentiality obligations substantially equivalent to those set forth herein;
1641: >
1642: > \(c\) to the extent required by applicable law, regulation, governmental order, subpoena, or other compulsory legal process, provided that the disclosing Party shall, to the extent legally permissible, provide the other Party with prompt written notice of such requirement prior to any such disclosure so as to afford the other Party an opportunity to seek a protective order or other appropriate remedy; and
1643: >
1644: > \(d\) in connection with any proceeding to enforce the terms of this Agreement.
1645: 
1646: In the event that either Party is required to disclose the existence or terms of this Agreement in response to a compulsory legal process as described in subsection (c) above, such Party shall disclose only such information as is strictly necessary to comply with such legal process and shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain confidential treatment of any information so disclosed.
1647: 
1648: **Section 4.2 --- Non-Disparagement**
1649: 
1650: Neither Party shall, directly or indirectly, make, publish, or cause to be made or published any disparaging, derogatory, or defamatory statements, whether oral or written, about the other Party, or about any of the other Party\'s shareholders, members, managers, officers, directors, employees, or agents, in connection with or relating to the Lawsuit, the MTSA, or the events and circumstances giving rise thereto. Nothing in this Section 4.2 shall be construed to prohibit either Party from providing truthful testimony or information in response to a lawful subpoena, court order, or governmental investigation, or from making truthful statements in connection with the enforcement of this Agreement.
1651: 
1652: **[ARTICLE V --- NO ADMISSION OF LIABILITY]{.underline}**
1653: 
1654: **Section 5.1 --- No Admission**
1655: 
1656: This Agreement constitutes a compromise and settlement of disputed claims and counterclaims. Neither the execution of this Agreement, the payment of the Settlement Amount, nor any of the terms, provisions, or conditions hereof shall be construed as, or deemed to be, an admission of liability, wrongdoing, fault, or responsibility by either Party with respect to any of the claims, counterclaims, allegations, or defenses asserted or that could have been asserted in the Lawsuit, or with respect to any other matter whatsoever. Each Party has entered into this Agreement solely for the purpose of avoiding the expense, burden, uncertainty, and distraction of continued litigation. This Agreement, the fact of its execution, and the Settlement Amount shall not be offered or received in evidence in any action, suit, or proceeding of any kind as an admission or concession of liability, fault, or wrongdoing by either Party, except that this Agreement may be offered or received in evidence in any proceeding brought to enforce its terms.
1657: 
1658: **[ARTICLE VI --- REPRESENTATIONS AND WARRANTIES]{.underline}**
1659: 
1660: **Section 6.1 --- Authority**
1661: 
1662: Each Party hereby represents and warrants to the other Party as follows:
1663: 
1664: > \(a\) Such Party is duly organized, validly existing, and in good standing under the laws of its state of organization, and has the full corporate or limited liability company power and authority to enter into, execute, deliver, and perform its obligations under this Agreement.
1665: >
1666: > \(b\) The execution, delivery, and performance of this Agreement by such Party have been duly authorized by all necessary corporate or limited liability company action, and the person executing this Agreement on behalf of such Party has been duly authorized to do so by all requisite corporate or company action, including any required approvals of such Party\'s board of directors, managers, or members, as applicable.
1667: >
1668: > \(c\) This Agreement constitutes the legal, valid, and binding obligation of such Party, enforceable against such Party in accordance with its terms, subject only to applicable bankruptcy, insolvency, reorganization, moratorium, and similar laws affecting creditors\' rights generally, and to general principles of equity (regardless of whether enforcement is sought in a proceeding at law or in equity).
1669: 
1670: **Section 6.2 --- No Assignment**
1671: 
1672: Each Party hereby represents and warrants to the other Party that it has not heretofore assigned, transferred, conveyed, pledged, hypothecated, or otherwise encumbered, in whole or in part, any claim, demand, cause of action, right, obligation, or interest that is the subject of the releases set forth in Article II, and that no other person or entity has any interest, by assignment, subrogation, or otherwise, in any such claim, demand, cause of action, right, obligation, or interest.
1673: 
1674: **Section 6.3 --- Voluntary Execution**
1675: 
1676: Each Party hereby represents and warrants to the other Party that: (i) it has had a full and fair opportunity to consult with legal counsel of its own choosing regarding the terms, meaning, and effect of this Agreement; (ii) it has in fact consulted with and been advised by its own legal counsel in connection with the negotiation, drafting, and execution of this Agreement; (iii) it has read, understands, and voluntarily accepts each and every provision of this Agreement; and (iv) it is executing this Agreement freely, voluntarily, and without duress, coercion, or undue influence of any kind. Each Party further acknowledges that it is not relying upon any statement, representation, promise, or inducement made by the other Party or the other Party\'s counsel, agents, or representatives, other than the express terms set forth in this Agreement, in deciding to enter into this Agreement.
1677: 
1678: **[ARTICLE VII --- GENERAL PROVISIONS]{.underline}**
1679: 
1680: **Section 7.1 --- Governing Law**
1681: 
1682: This Agreement shall be governed by, and construed and enforced in accordance with, the substantive laws of the State of Texas, without giving effect to any choice-of-law or conflict-of-laws rules, principles, or provisions (whether of the State of Texas or any other jurisdiction) that would cause the application of the laws of any jurisdiction other than the State of Texas.
1683: 
1684: **Section 7.2 --- Jurisdiction and Venue**

lines.text: **ORDER**
Upon consideration of the foregoing Stipulation of Dismissal with Prejudice, and good cause appearing therefor, **IT IS HEREBY ORDERED** that:

**1.** All claims, counterclaims, and cross-claims in this Action are **DISMISSED WITH PREJUDICE**, each Party to bear its own costs and attorneys\' fees except as otherwise provided in the Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release dated September 12, 2024.

**2.** This Court **RETAINS JURISDICTION** over the Parties and the subject matter of the Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release dated September 12, 2024, for the purpose of enforcing the terms and conditions thereof, including without limitation the permanent injunctive relief provisions, return and destruction obligations, non-solicitation covenant, and confidentiality provisions set forth therein.

**3.** The Preliminary Injunction entered by this Court on April 18, 2024, is hereby **DISSOLVED** and superseded by the terms of the Settlement Agreement and any consent permanent injunction order entered by this Court.
**4.** The Clerk of Court is directed to close this case and remove it from the active docket, subject to the Court\'s retained jurisdiction as set forth in Paragraph 2 above.
**SO ORDERED** this **\_** day of **\_\_\_**, 2024.
THE HONORABLE PATRICIA LANGFORD United States District Judge Southern District of Ohio, Eastern Division

**[SETTLEMENT AGREEMENT AND MUTUAL RELEASE]{.underline}**
**Effective Date: December 3, 2021**
This Settlement Agreement and Mutual Release (this \"Agreement\") is entered into as of December 3, 2021 (the \"Effective Date\"), by and between:
**CRESTLINE PACKAGING SOLUTIONS LLC**, an Ohio limited liability company, with its principal place of business at 4500 Needmore Road, Dayton, OH 45424 (\"CPS\");
and
**RIDGEWAY FREIGHT SERVICES INC.**, a Texas corporation, with its principal place of business at 7200 East Lancaster Avenue, Fort Worth, TX 76112 (\"Ridgeway\").
CPS and Ridgeway are each referred to herein individually as a \"Party\" and collectively as the \"Parties.\"
**[RECITALS]{.underline}**

**WHEREAS**, on April 15, 2019, CPS and Ridgeway entered into that certain Master Transportation Services Agreement (the \"MTSA\"), pursuant to which Ridgeway agreed to provide full truckload and less-than-truckload freight transportation services to CPS, including intrastate and interstate linehaul, cross-docking, and last-mile delivery services, in accordance with the rates, routes, and service levels specified therein;

**WHEREAS**, CPS terminated the MTSA effective April 22, 2021, pursuant to Section 9.2 thereof, following CPS\'s issuance of a thirty (30)-day written termination notice to Ridgeway on March 22, 2021;

**WHEREAS**, on or about June 7, 2021, CPS filed a lawsuit styled *Crestline Packaging Solutions LLC v. Ridgeway Freight Services Inc.*, Cause No. 342-2021-04871-TX, in the 342nd Judicial District Court of Tarrant County, Texas (the \"Lawsuit\"), asserting claims for breach of contract, money had and received, common-law fraud, and unjust enrichment, and seeking recovery of One Million Eight Hundred Forty-Seven Thousand Six Hundred Thirty-Two Dollars and Nineteen Cents (\$1,847,632.19) in alleged overcharges, together with contractual interest, attorneys\' fees, costs of court, and exemplary damages;

**WHEREAS**, Ridgeway filed a counterclaim in the Lawsuit asserting breach of contract based on CPS\'s alleged wrongful termination of the MTSA, seeking recovery of Three Hundred Forty Thousand Dollars (\$340,000.00) in alleged lost profits and related consequential damages;

**WHEREAS**, the Parties participated in a mediation before the Honorable Constance Farr, Judge (Ret.), at the Lone Star Dispute Resolution Center, 300 Throckmorton Street, Suite 1200, Fort Worth, TX 76102, on November 18, 2021, and, as a result of that mediation, reached an agreement in principle to resolve all claims and counterclaims asserted in the Lawsuit;

**WHEREAS**, the Parties desire to fully, finally, and forever resolve all disputes, controversies, claims, and counterclaims between them arising out of or relating to the MTSA, the Lawsuit, and any and all transactions and occurrences described therein, and to avoid the expense, burden, uncertainty, and distraction of further litigation; and

**NOW, THEREFORE**, in consideration of the mutual promises, covenants, and agreements set forth herein, and for other good and valuable consideration, the receipt and sufficiency of which are hereby acknowledged by each Party, the Parties agree as follows:
**[ARTICLE I --- SETTLEMENT PAYMENT]{.underline}**
**Section 1.1 --- Settlement Amount**

Ridgeway shall pay to CPS the total sum of One Million Five Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars (\$1,575,000.00) (the \"Settlement Amount\"), subject to and in accordance with the payment schedule set forth below:

> **(a) First Installment.** One Million Dollars (\$1,000,000.00) shall be due and payable within thirty (30) calendar days of the Effective Date (i.e., no later than January 2, 2022). Such payment shall be made by wire transfer of immediately available funds to a bank account designated in writing by CPS in accordance with Section 1.3 below.

> **(b) Second Installment.** Five Hundred Seventy-Five Thousand Dollars (\$575,000.00) shall be due and payable within ninety (90) calendar days of the Effective Date (i.e., no later than March 3, 2022). Such payment shall be made by wire transfer of immediately available funds to a bank account designated in writing by CPS in accordance with Section 1.3 below.

The Settlement Amount shall be allocated and reported for tax purposes in accordance with applicable law, and each Party shall be solely responsible for its own tax obligations arising from or relating to the receipt or payment of the Settlement Amount. Neither Party makes any representation or warranty to the other regarding the tax treatment or tax consequences of the Settlement Amount or any portion thereof.
**Section 1.2 --- Late Payment**

In the event that Ridgeway fails to make any installment payment when due as set forth in Section 1.1, interest shall accrue on the unpaid amount at the rate of one and one-half percent (1.5%) per month (eighteen percent (18%) per annum) from the applicable due date until such payment, together with all accrued interest thereon, is paid in full. Such interest shall compound monthly on the last calendar day of each month.

Upon any payment default by Ridgeway that remains uncured for ten (10) business days following written notice of such default from CPS to Ridgeway in accordance with Section 7.8, CPS shall be entitled, at its sole option and in addition to any other remedies available at law or in equity, to enter a consent judgment against Ridgeway in the amount of the entire unpaid balance of the Settlement Amount, plus all accrued and unpaid interest thereon, plus CPS\'s reasonable attorneys\' fees and costs incurred in connection with the enforcement of this Agreement (collectively, the \"Judgment Amount\"). Ridgeway hereby irrevocably consents to the entry of such judgment in the 342nd Judicial District Court of Tarrant County, Texas, and irrevocably waives any objection to personal jurisdiction, subject-matter jurisdiction, or venue in connection therewith. The Parties acknowledge that this consent judgment provision is a material inducement to CPS\'s agreement to accept installment payments rather than a single lump-sum payment, and that the enforcement rights set forth in this Section 1.2 are reasonable and necessary to protect CPS\'s legitimate interests under this Agreement.
**Section 1.3 --- Wire Instructions**

CPS shall provide Ridgeway with complete wire transfer instructions, including the name and address of the receiving financial institution, the ABA routing number, account name, and account number, within five (5) business days of the Effective Date. Ridgeway shall be entitled to rely on such instructions until CPS provides updated instructions in writing. Any change to wire transfer instructions must be confirmed by telephone by CPS\'s General Counsel or his designee prior to Ridgeway acting upon such changed instructions.
**[ARTICLE II --- MUTUAL RELEASES]{.underline}**
**Section 2.1 --- Release by CPS**

Effective upon CPS\'s receipt of the full Settlement Amount (including both the First Installment and the Second Installment as set forth in Section 1.1), CPS, on behalf of itself and its members, managers, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"CPS Releasing Parties\"), hereby fully, finally, unconditionally, and irrevocably releases, acquits, and forever discharges Ridgeway and its shareholders, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, insurers, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"Ridgeway Released Parties\") from any and all claims, demands, actions, causes of action, suits, debts, dues, sums of money, accounts, reckonings, bonds, bills, specialties, covenants, contracts, controversies, agreements, promises, variances, trespasses, judgments, executions, obligations, damages, losses, costs, expenses, and liabilities of every kind and nature whatsoever, whether at law or in equity, whether arising under statute, contract, tort, or otherwise, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, fixed or contingent, matured or unmatured, liquidated or unliquidated, that the CPS Releasing Parties ever had, now have, or hereafter may have against the Ridgeway Released Parties, from the beginning of the world through the Effective Date, arising out of, relating to, or in any way connected with: (i) the MTSA, including all amendments, schedules, and addenda thereto; (ii) the Lawsuit, including all claims, counterclaims, cross-claims, and defenses asserted or that could have been asserted therein; or (iii) the transactions, services, invoices, payments, disputes, negotiations, communications, and events described in or relating to the MTSA or the Lawsuit.
**Section 2.2 --- Release by Ridgeway**

Effective as of the Effective Date, Ridgeway, on behalf of itself and its shareholders, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, insurers, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"Ridgeway Releasing Parties\"), hereby fully, finally, unconditionally, and irrevocably releases, acquits, and forever discharges CPS and its members, managers, officers, directors, employees, agents, representatives, affiliates, successors, and assigns (collectively, the \"CPS Released Parties\") from any and all claims, demands, actions, causes of action, suits, debts, dues, sums of money, accounts, reckonings, bonds, bills, specialties, covenants, contracts, controversies, agreements, promises, variances, trespasses, judgments, executions, obligations, damages, losses, costs, expenses, and liabilities of every kind and nature whatsoever, whether at law or in equity, whether arising under statute, contract, tort, or otherwise, whether known or unknown, suspected or unsuspected, fixed or contingent, matured or unmatured, liquidated or unliquidated, that the Ridgeway Releasing Parties ever had, now have, or hereafter may have against the CPS Released Parties, from the beginning of the world through the Effective Date, arising out of, relating to, or in any way connected with: (i) the MTSA, including all amendments, schedules, and addenda thereto; (ii) the Lawsuit, including all claims, counterclaims, cross-claims, and defenses asserted or that could have been asserted therein; or (iii) the transactions, services, invoices, payments, disputes, negotiations, communications, and events described in or relating to the MTSA or the Lawsuit. Without limiting the generality of the foregoing, the release set forth in this Section 2.2 specifically encompasses and includes Ridgeway\'s counterclaim for alleged lost profits of Three Hundred Forty Thousand Dollars (\$340,000.00) and any and all other claims for damages, whether direct, indirect, consequential, incidental, ... The Parties acknowledge and agree that Ridgeway\'s release under this Section 2.2 is effective immediately upon the Effective Date and is not conditioned upon CPS\'s receipt of the Settlement Amount or any installment thereof.
**Section 2.3 --- Reservation**
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, the releases set forth therein shall not release, waive, or otherwise affect:

> \(b\) any claims, demands, actions, or causes of action arising from or related to a breach of this Agreement by either Party.
**[ARTICLE III --- DISMISSAL]{.underline}**
**Section 3.1 --- Dismissal**

Within ten (10) business days of the Effective Date, the Parties shall cause their respective counsel to jointly prepare, execute, and file an Agreed Order of Dismissal with Prejudice (the \"Dismissal Order\") in Cause No. 342-2021-04871-TX, pending in the 342nd Judicial District Court of Tarrant County, Texas. The Dismissal Order shall dismiss all of CPS\'s claims and all of Ridgeway\'s counterclaims with prejudice and without costs to either Party, with each Party bearing its own costs and attorneys\' fees except as otherwise expressly provided in this Agreement. Counsel for CPS, Calderwood & Harkness LLP, shall prepare the initial draft of the Dismissal Order and shall submit such draft to counsel for Ridgeway, Bartlett, Hogue & Sinclair LLP, for review and approval as to form prior to filing. Counsel for Ridgeway shall provide any comments or indicate approval as to form within five (5) business days of receipt of the draft Dismissal Order. The Parties shall cooperate fully and in good faith to secure entry of the Dismissal Order by the Court as expeditiously as practicable.
**[ARTICLE IV --- CONFIDENTIALITY]{.underline}**

The Parties agree that the existence and terms of this Agreement, including without limitation the Settlement Amount and the payment schedule, are and shall remain strictly confidential. > \(a\) to such Party\'s legal, financial, and tax advisors, including outside counsel, accountants, and tax preparers, who shall be informed of and bound by the confidentiality obligations set forth in this Section 4.1 as a condition of such disclosure;
> \(b\) to such Party\'s auditors, lenders, insurers, or investors, on a need-to-know basis and subject to appropriate confidentiality obligations substantially equivalent to those set forth herein;

> \(c\) to the extent required by applicable law, regulation, governmental order, subpoena, or other compulsory legal process, provided that the disclosing Party shall, to the extent legally permissible, provide the other Party with prompt written notice of such requirement prior to any such disclosure so as to afford the other Party an opportunity to seek a protective order or other appropriate remedy; and
> \(d\) in connection with any proceeding to enforce the terms of this Agreement.

In the event that either Party is required to disclose the existence or terms of this Agreement in response to a compulsory legal process as described in subsection (c) above, such Party shall disclose only such information as is strictly necessary to comply with such legal process and shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain confidential treatment of any information so disclosed.
**Section 4.2 --- Non-Disparagement**

> **(b) Second Installment.** Seven Hundred Fifty-Six Thousand Dollars (\$756,000.00), representing forty percent (40%) of the Settlement Amount, shall be due and payable within ninety (90) calendar days of the Effective Date, that is, no later than November 16, 2023.

**Federal income tax withholding.** Under IRC § 3401(a), the term \"wages\" includes all remuneration for services performed by an employee for an employer, including the cash value of all remuneration (including benefits) paid in any medium other than cash. The term encompasses back pay, severance pay, and amounts paid in settlement of employment-related claims that are in the nature of compensation for services. *See* Treas. Reg. § 31.3401(a)-1(a)(5). The settlement payment\'s wage component --- which substitutes for severance and bonus compensation --- falls squarely within this definition.

> If AMA uses the **percentage method**, withholding is computed based on Aldrich\'s most recent Form W-4 on file with AMA. However, because Aldrich\'s employment was terminated on October 14, 2022, and more than one year will have elapsed before the settlement payment is made, AMA should confirm whether it has a valid W-4 on file or whether Aldrich should be asked to submit a new W-4 in connection with the settlement payment.

> **Attorneys\' fees component.** Aldrich claimed \$750,000 in attorneys\' fees incurred in prosecuting his claims against AMA. Under IRC § 62(a)(20), an above-the-line deduction is available for attorneys\' fees and court costs paid by a taxpayer in connection with certain employment-related claims, including claims of unlawful discrimination and certain whistleblower claims. To the extent Aldrich\'s claims fall within the scope of § 62(a)(20), he may deduct attorneys\' fees on his individual tax return regardless of how the settlement payment is characterized. The Settlement Agreement does not separately allocate attorneys\' fees; rather, they are subsumed in the non-wage component. Aldrich\'s counsel, Cameron Whitfield, has indicated that Whitfield & Associates\' fee arrangement with Aldrich is a 33.3% contingency fee, and that Whitfield & Associates intends to issue a Form 1099 to Aldrich for the portion of the settlement allocable to attorneys\' fees if required. AMA\'s reporting obligations with respect to the attorneys\' fees component are limited to accurately reporting the non-wage component on Form 1099-MISC.

Because the non-wage component is not in the nature of \"wages\" as defined in IRC § 3401(a), it is **not subject to federal income tax withholding or FICA taxes**. The withholding obligation under IRC § 3402 applies only to \"wages\" --- that is, amounts paid for services rendered in an employer-employee relationship. Settlement payments that are in the nature of damages, general settlement consideration, or non-compensatory payments do not fall within the definition of wages, even if they are taxable income to the recipient. *See* Rev. Rul. 80-364, 1980-2 C.B. 294 (distinguishing between settlement payments that are wages subject to withholding and those that are not).

AMA must report the \$1,292,500 non-wage component on a **Form 1099-MISC** (Miscellaneous Information). The payment should be reported in **box 3** (\"Other income\") of Form 1099-MISC. Box 3 is the appropriate reporting box for settlement payments that constitute taxable income to the recipient but are not wages, nonemployee compensation, rents, royalties, or other specifically categorized income. The payment should not be reported on Form 1099-NEC (Nonemployee Compensation), as Aldrich is not providing services to AMA in connection with the settlement, and characterization of the non-wage component as \"nonemployee compensation\" would be inaccurate and could subject AMA to penalties for incorrect information reporting.

Additionally, if any portion of the non-wage component is paid to Aldrich\'s counsel (Whitfield & Associates) --- for example, if the settlement payment is directed to Whitfield & Associates\' client trust account --- AMA may be required to issue a separate Form 1099-MISC to Whitfield & Associates for the portion of the payment received by the law firm. Under Treas. Reg. § 1.6045-5(a), the payor of a settlement payment must generally report the payment to the attorney if the payment is made to the attorney\'s trust account or if the attorney\'s name is on the settlement check. AMA should confirm the payment arrangements and issue 1099s accordingly.

The IRS retains the authority to challenge the tax allocation of settlement payments if it determines that the allocation does not reflect the economic substance of the settlement. While the IRS generally respects an allocation agreed upon by adverse parties in an arm\'s-length negotiation, it is not bound by the parties\' characterization if the allocation is inconsistent with the substance of the underlying claims. *See* *Robinson v. Commissioner*, 102 T.C. 116, 130--31 (1994) (holding that the Tax Court will look to the \"nature of the claim that was the actual basis for settlement\" to determine the tax treatment of settlement proceeds, and that while an express allocation in a settlement agreement is \"strong evidence\" of the parties\' intent, the IRS may look behind the allocation if it is inconsistent with the economic substance).

In *Bagley v. Commissioner*, T.C. Memo 2014-30, the Tax Court reiterated the principle that the tax treatment of settlement payments is determined by the nature and basis of the underlying claims, and that the parties\' allocation will be respected if it reflects a genuine, arm\'s-length negotiation and is consistent with the damages theories advanced in the litigation. **AMA\'s deduction.** The allocation also has implications for AMA\'s tax deductions. AMA may deduct the wage component (\$1,057,500) as an ordinary and necessary business expense under IRC § 162(a), as compensation paid to an employee (or former employee) in connection with the resolution of employment-related claims. The non-wage component (\$1,292,500) may also be deductible under IRC § 162(a) as a settlement payment arising from AMA\'s business operations, provided the settlement is not characterized as a penalty or fine within the meaning of IRC § 162(f). Section 162(f) denies a deduction for any amount paid or incurred to or at the direction of a government (or specified nongovernmental entity) in relation to the violation of any law or the investigation or inquiry by a governmental entity into the potential violation of any law. Because the Aldrich settlement is a private settlement between AMA and a former employee, and does not involve any government-directed payment, the § 162(f) limitation does not apply. The full \$2,350,000 cash settlement payment should therefore be deductible by AMA as an ordinary and necessary business expense under § 162(a).

**C.** On September 18, 2022, Hurricane Callista, classified by the National Hurricane Center as a Category 4 hurricane on the Saffir-Veltason Hurricane Wind Scale, made landfall in the Lower Florida Keys with maximum sustained winds of approximately 145 miles per hour and produced storm surge inundation of approximately eight (8) to fourteen (14) feet above normal tide levels in Monroe County and approximately six (6) to ten (10) feet above normal tide levels in Lee County. Hurricane Callista caused catastrophic and widespread damage throughout southern Florida, including significant damage to coastal structures, resort properties, marinas, and critical infrastructure along the Florida Keys and the Gulf Coast of southwestern Florida. On February 10, 2023, Pinnacle, through its coverage counsel, Fendowell Rourke & Stanton LLP, followed Ironclad\'s denial on a follow-form basis and denied coverage for VHG\'s business-interruption claim to the extent it fell within Pinnacle\'s layer. Montclair and Sovereign Re, through their joint coverage counsel, Delvecchio & Kraus LLP, did not issue formal denials of coverage but reserved all rights under their respective policies, asserting that their excess layers would not be reached based on the application of the named-windstorm sub-limit asserted by Ironclad and Pinnacle.

The purpose of this memorandum is to provide Verimark Hospitality Group Inc. (\"VHG\" or the \"Company\") with a comprehensive analysis of settlement ranges, litigation risks, and our recommended settlement authority in advance of the court-ordered mediation currently scheduled for December 4--5, 2023. The mediation will be conducted before the Honorable Richard Mendelson (Ret.) at Keystone Dispute Resolution Inc., located at 200 S. Biscayne Boulevard, Suite 3100, Miami, Florida 33131. The mediation fee is \$15,000 per day for the two-day session, to be split among the parties pursuant to the court\'s November 20, 2023 order.

VHG\'s total claimed losses in this action are \$60,000,000 in business-interruption (\"BI\") losses arising from Hurricane Callista, a Category 4 hurricane that made landfall on September 18, 2022, in the Lower Florida Keys. The losses are distributed across three VHG-owned and operated hospitality properties: Grand Key Resort (\$31.4 million), Harborview Hotel & Conference Center (\$18.7 million), and Sunset Shores (\$9.9 million). VHG seeks recovery under an insurance tower providing \$60 million in total limits above a \$500,000 deductible, comprised of the following layers:

Based on our thorough analysis of the coverage issues, the current state of the evidence, the relative strengths and vulnerabilities of VHG\'s position, the projected costs of continued litigation through trial, and the anticipated settlement posture of each defendant carrier, we recommend that VHG authorize settlement for no less than **\$40,000,000** (representing 66.7% of the claimed \$60 million), with a **target settlement range of \$45,000,000 to \$50,000,000**.

The rationale for this recommendation, elaborated in detail below, rests on several key considerations. VHG holds a strong position on the most consequential coverage issue in the case --- the deletion of the \$15 million windstorm sub-limit at the July 2022 policy renewal. However, VHG faces meaningful litigation risk on the concurrent causation and flood exclusion issues, as well as the period-of-restoration disputes, which could reduce recovery in the range of \$9 million to \$20 million depending on how these issues are resolved at trial. Additionally, trial is unlikely to occur before late 2024, and the continued expenditure of legal fees and costs --- projected at \$1.75 million to \$2.4 million through trial --- along with the attendant uncertainty for a publicly traded company (Nasdaq: VMRK) weigh in favor of resolution at the mediation.

VHG filed its Complaint against Ironclad Indemnity Corporation (\"Ironclad\"), Pinnacle Surplus Lines Inc. (\"Pinnacle\"), Montclair Assurance Company (\"Montclair\"), and Sovereign Re Ltd. (\"Sovereign Re\") on March 1, 2023, in the Eleventh Judicial Circuit of Florida, Miami-Dade County. The case has been assigned to the Honorable Catherine Embry, Circuit Judge, and bears Case Number 2022-CA-031547. The Complaint asserts claims for breach of contract, declaratory judgment, and bad faith against the defendant insurers, seeking recovery of \$60 million in business-interruption losses under the respective insurance policies.

The case has proceeded through a robust discovery period. Fact discovery was completed on September 30, 2023, pursuant to the court\'s revised scheduling order. During the fact discovery period, the parties conducted depositions of key witnesses on both sides, exchanged approximately 187,000 pages of documents, and engaged in multiple rounds of written discovery. Expert reports were served simultaneously on September 15, 2023, with VHG\'s damages expert, Dr. Helen Vasquez of Meridian Forensic Economics, providing a comprehensive quantification of VHG\'s BI losses at \$60 million, and defendants\' expert, Dr. Warren Birk of Graystone Consulting Group LLC, providing a competing analysis estimating VHG\'s losses in the range of \$28 million to \$35 million. Rebuttal expert reports were served on October 2, 2023.

VHG\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment regarding the deletion of the windstorm sub-limit was filed on November 1, 2023. The motion is supported by a comprehensive Memorandum of Law, a Statement of Undisputed Material Facts, and declarations from three key witnesses: Sandra Pellegrini (VHG\'s Vice President of Risk Management), Franklin Orde (Account Executive at Tidewater Risk Advisors, VHG\'s insurance broker), and Dr. Helen Vasquez (VHG\'s damages expert). The motion argues that the undisputed evidence --- including the broker\'s deposition testimony, the renewal correspondence, the binder language, and the premium increase --- establishes as a matter of law that the windstorm sub-limit was deleted at the July 2022 renewal.

VHG\'s Opposition to Defendants\' Cross-Motion is due to be filed on November 29, 2023. As of the date of this memorandum, our team is finalizing that opposition. The opposition will argue that defendants\' cross-motion ignores the binding effect of the renewal binder, the underwriter\'s course of dealing, and the well-established Florida principle that ambiguities in insurance policies are construed against the insurer.

**Montclair Assurance Company and Sovereign Re Ltd.** are jointly represented by Delvecchio & Kraus LLP. The defense team is led by Patricia Kraus, a partner with a national insurance defense practice. She is supported by Raymond Cho, a senior associate. Ms. Kraus has adopted a somewhat less adversarial posture than Mr. Stanton in the litigation to date, consistent with the fact that both Montclair and Sovereign Re reserved their rights but never formally denied VHG\'s claim. Their position has been that their respective excess layers would not be reached if the windstorm sub-limit applied, effectively deferring to the sub-limit issue as the threshold question.

This section provides a detailed analysis of each contested coverage issue, including an assessment of VHG\'s likelihood of prevailing on each issue and the potential impact on the overall recovery. These assessments are necessarily based on professional judgment and are informed by the current state of the evidence, the applicable law, and our experience with similar disputes in Florida courts.

This is the single most consequential issue in the case. If the \$15 million named-windstorm sub-limit applies, VHG\'s maximum BI recovery from the insurance tower is capped at \$15 million (less the \$500,000 deductible), regardless of the outcome on any other coverage issue. Conversely, if the sub-limit is deemed deleted, the full \$60 million tower of coverage is available to VHG, subject to the other defenses discussed below.
**1. VHG\'s Position (Strong)**

VHG contends that the \$15 million named-windstorm sub-limit contained in the Ironclad primary policy (Policy No. IIC-PRP-2022-07541) was deleted during the July 2022 policy renewal. VHG\'s position is supported by substantial evidence developed during discovery:

**Broker Testimony.** Franklin Orde, the account executive at Tidewater Risk Advisors responsible for VHG\'s account, testified in his deposition on August 28, 2023, that during the July 2022 renewal negotiations, Ironclad\'s underwriter, Janet Moreno, agreed to delete the named-windstorm sub-limit in exchange for an increase in the annual premium. Mr. Orde testified that this agreement was reached during a telephone call on June 22, 2022, and was subsequently confirmed in an email exchange between Mr. Orde and Ms. Moreno on June 23, 2022. The June 23 email, produced in discovery as Document VHG-00024517, reflects Mr. Orde\'s summary of the agreed-upon renewal terms, including the notation \"Named Windstorm sub-limit --- DELETED per agreement.\" Ms. Moreno responded to this email the same day, stating: \"Confirmed. Please proceed with renewal on these terms.\"

**Policyholder Testimony.** Sandra Pellegrini, VHG\'s Vice President of Risk Management, testified in her deposition on August 14, 2023, that she had specifically requested the deletion of the windstorm sub-limit as part of the July 2022 renewal, given VHG\'s increased exposure to hurricane risk across its Florida portfolio. Ms. Pellegrini testified that VHG understood the sub-limit was removed and relied upon that understanding in structuring the insurance tower and making business decisions regarding the retention of risk.

**Documentary Evidence.** In addition to the broker correspondence referenced above, the renewal binder issued by Ironclad on July 12, 2022 (Document IIC-00008734), does not reference the \$15 million named-windstorm sub-limit. While the binder does not affirmatively state that the sub-limit was deleted, the omission of the sub-limit from the binder --- which had been expressly included in the prior year\'s binder --- is consistent with VHG\'s position that deletion was agreed upon.

**Premium Increase.** The total annual aggregate premium for VHG\'s insurance tower increased at the July 2022 renewal, from \$1,620,000 in the prior policy year to \$1,840,000. The premium breakdown is as follows: Ironclad primary --- \$980,000; Pinnacle first excess --- \$410,000; Montclair second excess --- \$265,000; Sovereign Re third excess --- \$185,000. The magnitude of the premium increase is consistent with the removal of the windstorm sub-limit, which would have expanded the effective coverage available under the tower for named-windstorm events.

**Declaration of Franklin Orde.** A declaration from Mr. Orde was filed in support of VHG\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment, attesting under penalty of perjury to the facts described above and authenticating the relevant correspondence.
We assess the probability that VHG prevails on the windstorm sub-limit issue at **approximately 65--70%**. Several factors support this assessment:

> • Florida law firmly establishes the principle of *contra proferentem* --- that ambiguities in insurance policies are construed against the insurer that drafted the policy. The discrepancy between the broker correspondence (confirming deletion) and the policy-as-issued (retaining the sub-limit) creates, at minimum, an ambiguity that should be resolved in VHG\'s favor.

> • Notably, Mr. Haddon\'s deposition testimony revealed that Ironclad\'s internal claims committee had debated whether the sub-limit was effectively deleted during the renewal process. This internal uncertainty undermines the credibility of Ironclad\'s categorical assertion that the sub-limit applies and may suggest that Ironclad\'s claims personnel recognized the strength of VHG\'s position.

**upside scenario:** If the court grants VHG\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment, the sub-limit issue is removed from the case entirely, and VHG proceeds to trial (or settlement negotiations) with the full \$60 million tower available. This would fundamentally reshape the defendants\' settlement posture and likely result in a significantly higher settlement.

**Downside scenario:** If the court grants the defendants\' Cross-Motion for Partial Summary Judgment, VHG\'s recovery from the insurance tower is capped at \$15 million less the \$500,000 deductible, or \$14.5 million. This would effectively render the excess layers unreachable and would collapse VHG\'s claim into a single-carrier dispute with Ironclad.

The storm surge associated with Hurricane Callista was significant. According to data published by the National Hurricane Center (\"NHC\"), storm surge levels in Monroe County (the location of Grand Key Resort) reached 8 to 14 feet above normal tide levels during the landfall event. The storm surge at the Grand Key property caused extensive damage to ground-floor areas, the marina, and certain landscaping and infrastructure elements, while wind damage was sustained throughout the property, including to upper floors, roofing systems, and building envelopes.
**2. VHG\'s Position**

VHG argues that Florida\'s efficient proximate cause doctrine applies under governing Florida law and that the ACC clause, to the extent it purports to override this doctrine, is unenforceable as a matter of public policy. VHG contends that the named windstorm --- Hurricane Callista --- was the efficient proximate cause of the damage at all three properties, and that the storm surge was merely a consequence of the windstorm, not an independent excluded peril.

In support of this position, VHG retained Jeffrey Caldwell, PE, of Caldwell Engineering Associates Inc., Doral, Florida, to prepare a forensic engineering report differentiating wind damage from storm-surge damage at each of the three affected properties. Mr. Caldwell\'s report, produced in discovery on August 15, 2023, concludes that:

VHG argues that even under the ACC clause --- assuming it is enforceable --- wind damage is independently covered because it constitutes a distinct and separable cause of loss from the storm surge. Under this theory, VHG is entitled to full recovery for all wind-related damage, with the storm-surge damage excluded or separately addressed.
We assess the probability that VHG prevails on the concurrent causation / flood exclusion issue at **approximately 55--60%**. This assessment reflects the following considerations:

> • The strength of VHG\'s position on this issue depends in significant part on the court\'s willingness to disaggregate wind damage from storm-surge damage, as Mr. Caldwell\'s report proposes. If the court accepts this disaggregation approach, the flood exclusion would apply only to the separately identifiable storm-surge damage, preserving coverage for the wind-related losses. If the court instead applies the ACC clause broadly, coverage could be barred for all damage at locations where storm surge was a concurrent cause.

The policy provides business-interruption coverage for the \"period of restoration,\" defined as the period beginning with the date of the physical loss or damage and ending when the property is repaired, rebuilt, or replaced \"with reasonable speed and similar quality.\" Ironclad argues that BI coverage terminates when repairs \"could have been completed with reasonable speed,\" not necessarily when VHG actually completed the repairs. The practical significance of this dispute is that Ironclad contends VHG unreasonably extended the restoration period at two of the three properties, and that BI coverage should be calculated based on a shorter period.

> • **Grand Key Resort** was closed for 178 days (September 18, 2022 through March 15, 2023), but could have been restored and reopened 30 to 45 days earlier with expedited contractor scheduling and more aggressive project management. Ms. Whitford testified in her deposition on July 24, 2023, that comparable hospitality properties in the Florida Keys restored operations more quickly following Hurricane Callista.
**2. VHG\'s Position**

VHG contends that the restoration timelines at all three properties were reasonable in light of the extraordinary circumstances created by a Category 4 hurricane. Specifically, VHG has presented evidence that:

> • Contractor shortages were severe in the affected areas following Hurricane Callista. Marcus Ellsworth, VHG\'s Chief Executive Officer, testified in his deposition on August 7, 2023, about the difficulty of securing qualified contractors in the Florida Keys, where the labor pool was already limited and was overwhelmed by the demand for restoration services across the region. Mr. Ellsworth testified that VHG solicited bids from over a dozen general contractors and that only two submitted proposals within the first 30 days following the hurricane.

> • Permitting delays imposed by Monroe County and Lee County contributed to the extended restoration periods. VHG provided documentation showing that building permit applications submitted in October 2022 were not processed until November and December 2022, due to the volume of post-hurricane applications.

> • Supply-chain disruptions affected the availability of building materials, including roofing materials, impact-resistant windows, and commercial HVAC components. Diane Calder, VHG\'s Chief Financial Officer, testified in her deposition on August 8, 2023, about the financial constraints and decision-making around restoration timing, including the Company\'s decision to prioritize quality and code-compliant repairs over speed.

> • Dr. Helen Vasquez\'s expert report included sensitivity analyses demonstrating that even under the shortened restoration periods proposed by defendants, VHG\'s total BI losses exceed \$50 million. This analysis significantly mitigates the impact of this issue, as it shows that the period-of-restoration dispute affects only a modest portion of the total claim.

We assess the probability that VHG prevails on the full restoration period at **approximately 60%**. VHG\'s position is reasonable and well-supported by the evidence, but defendants have a colorable argument that some acceleration of the restoration timeline was feasible, particularly at Grand Key Resort.

Even if the court accepts defendants\' shorter restoration theory, the reduction in the BI claim would be modest --- approximately **\$4 million to \$7 million** from the total \$60 million claim. This is because the shortened restoration periods proposed by defendants (30--45 days for Grand Key, 20--30 days for Harborview) represent a relatively small fraction of the total closure periods, and VHG\'s revenue loss during those incremental days, while significant, does not fundamentally alter the magnitude of the claim.

Ironclad has asserted as an affirmative defense that VHG failed to take reasonable steps to reduce the period of business interruption. Specifically, defendants allege that VHG could have arranged temporary facilities, executed partial reopenings more quickly, or made alternative arrangements for displaced guests and conference bookings that would have reduced the magnitude of the BI losses.
**2. VHG\'s Position**
VHG has a strong factual record of mitigation efforts. The evidence shows that VHG took affirmative steps to mitigate its losses, including:

> • **Redirection of bookings** to unaffected sister properties in VHG\'s portfolio, including properties in the Tampa Bay area and on the Atlantic coast. Sandra Pellegrini testified about the coordination of this effort, including outreach to guests with existing reservations and the establishment of a dedicated customer-service team to manage rebookings.

We assess the probability that defendants prevail on the failure-to-mitigate defense at **approximately 15--20%**. This defense is weak given VHG\'s strong factual record of mitigation efforts. Even if a court were to find some deficiency in VHG\'s mitigation efforts, the potential reduction in the BI claim would be modest --- approximately **\$2 million to \$4 million** --- and would likely overlap with the period-of-restoration adjustment discussed in Section III.C above.

Under this scenario, VHG prevails on the windstorm sub-limit issue and largely prevails on the period-of-restoration and mitigation disputes, but the court accepts some allocation of Grand Key Resort losses to flood/storm surge under the ACC clause, resulting in a modest reduction.

Under this scenario, VHG prevails on the windstorm sub-limit issue, but the court accepts defendants\' position on a meaningful portion of the concurrent causation / flood exclusion and period-of-restoration disputes. The Grand Key Resort recovery is reduced by the flood allocation, and the Harborview recovery is modestly reduced by the period-of-restoration adjustment.

Under this scenario, the court upholds the \$15 million windstorm sub-limit, capping VHG\'s named-windstorm BI recovery at \$14.5 million (after deductible). VHG may recover some additional amounts for non-windstorm-related BI losses, but the total recovery is substantially reduced.

> • **Expert costs incurred:** VHG has retained Dr. Helen Vasquez and her team at Meridian Forensic Economics (Dr. Vasquez at \$625/hour; supporting analysts at \$375/hour), as well as Jeffrey Caldwell, PE, of Caldwell Engineering Associates Inc. Expert costs through November 2023 are included in the expenses figure above.

If the case does not settle at the December mediation and proceeds through trial --- which we estimate would not occur until late 2024, based on the current pace of the litigation and the court\'s calendar --- VHG should anticipate the following additional costs:

**Cost savings.** Settlement at the December mediation would save VHG approximately \$1,750,000 to \$2,400,000 in additional legal fees, expert costs, and litigation expenses that would otherwise be incurred through trial.

**Time value of money.** A settlement reached in December 2023 or early 2024 would provide VHG with recovery funds approximately 6 to 12 months sooner than a post-trial judgment, which would not be entered until late 2024 at the earliest and could be subject to post-trial motions and appeal, potentially extending the timeline by an additional 12 to 24 months. Assuming a discount rate of 5--7% (reflecting VHG\'s cost of capital), the present value of a \$45 million settlement received in January 2024 exceeds the present value of a \$48 million judgment received in December 2024.

**Public company considerations.** VHG is a publicly traded company (Nasdaq: VMRK). Early resolution of this litigation would reduce uncertainty for investors and analysts, improve VHG\'s ability to provide forward-looking guidance in its earnings reports, and simplify VHG\'s SEC reporting obligations with respect to contingent liabilities. Settlement would also avoid the risk of adverse trial publicity, which could affect VHG\'s stock price, brand reputation, and relationships with guests and corporate clients.

Pinnacle followed Ironclad\'s denial of VHG\'s claim on February 10, 2023, but has an independent obligation to assess coverage under its own policy. Pinnacle is jointly represented with Ironclad by Fendowell Rourke & Stanton LLP, which facilitates coordinated settlement negotiations.

Montclair provides the second excess layer of \$10 million in excess of \$40 million, under Policy No. MAC-XS2-2022-09817. Montclair reserved its rights upon receipt of VHG\'s claim but never issued a formal denial, maintaining a less adversarial posture than Ironclad and Pinnacle throughout the litigation. Montclair is represented by Delvecchio & Kraus LLP, with Patricia Kraus as lead counsel and Raymond Cho as senior associate.

As the highest layer in the tower, Sovereign Re has the strongest argument for a substantial discount in any settlement allocation. Its \$50 million attachment point means that its layer is reached only if VHG\'s total covered losses exceed \$50 million --- a result that requires VHG to prevail on essentially all coverage issues. Conversely, if the sub-limit is stricken and VHG prevails on the concurrent causation and period-of-restoration issues (even partially), Sovereign Re faces meaningful exposure.

The mediation is scheduled for two days: **December 4--5, 2023**. It will be held at Keystone\'s offices at 200 S. Biscayne Boulevard, Suite 3100, Miami, Florida 33131. The mediation fee is \$15,000 per day, for a total of \$30,000 for the two-day session. Pursuant to the court\'s November 20, 2023 order, the mediation fee is to be split among the parties, with VHG bearing one-half and the defendants collectively bearing the other half.

**Opening Demand: \$60 Million (Full Policy Limits).** VHG should open the mediation with a demand for the full \$60 million in policy limits, demonstrating confidence in the strength of the claim and establishing the high end of the negotiating range. While we do not expect to settle at this level, a strong opening demand signals to the mediator and to the defendants that VHG is prepared to proceed to trial and believes in the merits of its case.

**Mediation Position Statement.** A confidential mediation position statement will be submitted to Judge Mendelson by November 28, 2023, in accordance with his standard mediation procedures. The position statement will provide a comprehensive summary of the facts, the coverage issues, the damages analysis, and VHG\'s litigation position. It will be marked \"CONFIDENTIAL --- FOR MEDIATOR\'S EYES ONLY\" and will not be shared with the defendants.

**Leverage from Pending PSJ Motion.** We will emphasize to the defendants and to the mediator that VHG\'s pending Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on the windstorm sub-limit issue has not yet been decided by the court. If the court grants VHG\'s motion, the defendants\' settlement posture will deteriorate significantly, as the full \$60 million tower will be available and the excess carriers will face full-layer exposure. The pendency of this motion creates a \"ticking clock\" dynamic that should motivate the defendants to resolve the case before the court rules.

**Target Range: \$45 Million to \$50 Million.** Our target for the mediation is to negotiate a settlement in the range of \$45 million to \$50 million, which represents the upper half of the aggregate settlement range estimated in Section VI.E. We believe this range is achievable given the strength of VHG\'s position on the sub-limit issue, the bad-faith leverage, and the mediator\'s likely assessment that a trial outcome in the \$40--\$55 million range is more probable than not.

**Walk-Away Floor: \$40 Million.** We recommend that VHG establish a firm walk-away floor of \$40 million. If the mediation does not produce an offer at or above this level, VHG should be prepared to proceed with the litigation, including the pending summary judgment motions and, if necessary, trial.
**[C. VHG Representatives at Mediation]{.underline}**
We recommend that the following VHG representatives attend the mediation:

> • **Diane Calder, Chief Financial Officer** --- to address any financial questions that may arise during the negotiation, including questions about the BI calculations, VHG\'s financial condition, and the impact of settlement on VHG\'s financial reporting.

Both Mr. Driscoll and Ms. Calder should attend with full settlement authority within the range approved by the VHG Board of Directors. Marcus Ellsworth, VHG\'s Chief Executive Officer, should be available by telephone throughout the mediation session in the event that his participation is needed for any discussions that exceed the scope of Mr. Driscoll\'s and Ms. Calder\'s authority.
Calderwood & Harkness\'s engagement with VHG in this matter is governed by the engagement letter dated August 15, 2022, as amended. The fee structure includes the following components:

**Contingency Enhancement.** In addition to hourly fees, the engagement letter provides for a contingency enhancement equal to 5% of net recovery above \$30 million. This enhancement was negotiated to align the firm\'s incentives with VHG\'s goal of maximizing recovery and reflects the risk that Calderwood & Harkness assumed in committing substantial resources to this case. The enhancement applies to any recovery, whether by settlement, judgment, or otherwise.
**[B. Net Recovery to VHG at Various Settlement Levels]{.underline}**
The following table summarizes VHG\'s estimated net recovery at various settlement levels, after deducting hourly fees, the contingency enhancement, and expenses:
**Settlement**   **Hourly Fees**   **Enhancement**   **Expenses**   **Net to VHG**       **Net as % of \$60M Claim**

These net recovery figures should be compared against the expected net recovery through trial. If VHG proceeds to trial and obtains a judgment at the probability-weighted expected value of approximately \$45.3 million, the additional litigation costs of \$1.75 million to \$2.4 million would reduce the net recovery to approximately \$38.5 million to \$39.5 million (after total fees, enhancement, and expenses of approximately \$5.3 million to \$6.1 million), and the recovery would not be received until late 2024 at the earliest. This comparison further supports settlement at the recommended levels.

1\. **Settlement Authority Floor: \$40,000,000.** We recommend that VHG establish a settlement authority floor of \$40,000,000 in aggregate from all defendant carriers. This figure represents the minimum settlement that VHG should accept at the December mediation.

2\. **Target Settlement Range: \$45,000,000 to \$50,000,000.** We recommend that VHG\'s negotiating team target a settlement in the range of \$45 million to \$50 million, which represents the upper half of the estimated aggregate settlement range and exceeds the probability-weighted expected value of the litigation.

3\. **Opening Mediation Demand: \$60,000,000.** VHG should open the mediation with a demand for the full \$60 million claim amount, consistent with the strength of VHG\'s position and the need to establish a strong negotiating anchor.

> \(a\) **Exceeds net expected value of trial.** A settlement of \$40 million at the mediation exceeds the probability-weighted expected value of the litigation (\$42--\$47 million gross, reduced to approximately \$38.5--\$39.5 million net after additional trial costs of \$1.75--\$2.4 million). A settlement at or above \$40 million thus delivers value to VHG that is equal to or greater than what VHG can expect to achieve through trial, without the attendant risks.

> \(b\) **Meaningful net recovery.** At \$40 million, VHG\'s net recovery after all fees, enhancements, and expenses is approximately \$36.4 million, representing recovery of 60.7% of the \$60 million gross claim after costs. This is a meaningful and substantial recovery that reflects the strength of VHG\'s coverage position.

> \(c\) **Eliminates downside risk.** Settlement at \$40 million eliminates the risk of an adverse ruling on the windstorm sub-limit issue (Scenarios 4 and 5 in the scenario analysis), which could reduce VHG\'s recovery to a range of \$8 million to \$25 million. The sub-limit issue, while favorable to VHG, carries a 30--35% probability of an adverse outcome. The elimination of this tail risk is itself a significant benefit of settlement.

> \(d\) **Certainty and timeliness.** Settlement provides VHG with a certain and timely recovery, avoiding the uncertainty and delay of continued litigation through trial and potential appeal. VHG would receive settlement funds in early 2024, approximately 6 to 12 months sooner than a post-trial judgment.

> \(e\) **Public company considerations.** As a publicly traded company on the Nasdaq exchange (VMRK), VHG has significant interest in resolving the uncertainty associated with this litigation. Early resolution simplifies VHG\'s financial reporting, reduces the need for contingent-liability disclosures, and avoids potential adverse publicity from a trial. Settlement provides certainty for investors and analysts and permits VHG\'s management to focus on operational priorities.

5\. **Against Settling Below \$40 Million.** We recommend against settling below \$40 million absent a material adverse development in the litigation, such as an adverse ruling on VHG\'s Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on the windstorm sub-limit or the emergence of new evidence that materially weakens VHG\'s position on the concurrent causation or period-of-restoration issues. No such developments are anticipated at this time.

6\. **Board Authorization.** We request that the VHG Board of Directors, or such officer(s) as may be authorized to approve settlement on behalf of the Company, approve the recommended settlement authority range of \$40 million to \$50 million prior to the December 4, 2023 mediation. Written confirmation of such authorization should be provided to Calderwood & Harkness no later than December 1, 2023.

1\. **Finalize Confidential Mediation Position Statement.** Calderwood & Harkness will finalize and submit the confidential mediation position statement to Judge Mendelson by **November 28, 2023**. A draft of the position statement will be circulated to the VHG team for review and comment by November 26, 2023.

3\. **Obtain Written Settlement Authority.** VHG should obtain written settlement authority from the Board of Directors or the authorized representative(s) approving the recommended settlement range of \$40 million to \$50 million. This authorization should be in writing and should be provided to Calderwood & Harkness no later than **December 1, 2023**.

4\. **Pre-Mediation Client Conference Call.** We recommend scheduling a pre-mediation conference call with the VHG client team --- including Nathaniel Driscoll (General Counsel), Diane Calder (CFO), and Sandra Pellegrini (VP, Risk Management) --- during the **week of November 27, 2023**. This call will cover final mediation strategy, anticipated negotiation dynamics, and any remaining questions regarding the settlement authority analysis.

5\. **Coordinate Attendance at Mediation.** Confirm attendance and logistics for the mediation at Keystone Dispute Resolution Inc., 200 S. Biscayne Boulevard, Suite 3100, Miami, Florida 33131, on **December 4--5, 2023**. We will coordinate hotel accommodations and travel arrangements for VHG representatives as needed.

6\. **File VHG\'s Opposition to Defendants\' Cross-Motion.** Our team will finalize and file VHG\'s Opposition to Defendants\' Cross-Motion for Partial Summary Judgment by **November 29, 2023**, ensuring that this brief is on file with the court before the mediation and available to reference during negotiations.

Verimark Hospitality Group Inc., a Delaware corporation, publicly traded on the Nasdaq Stock Market under the ticker symbol \"VMRK,\" with its principal offices located at 1900 Brickell Avenue, Suite 3200, Miami, Florida 33129 (hereinafter referred to as \"VHG\" or \"Plaintiff\").
